variants.title: Run the bucket
variants.context: A token bucket stores up to b credits and refills at r per second. An operation with cost c is admitted only when c tokens are available. Over an interval T, a conforming flow cannot exceed r×T + b.
variants.prompt: Refill is 10 tokens per second and capacity is 50. The bucket is full when 80 requests of cost 1 arrive at once. How many are admitted immediately?
variants.hint: Only stored credit can be spent instantly.
variants.explanation: 50 tokens are stored, so 50 requests pass; the other 30 wait for refill or are rejected.

mistakes.feedback: Ten per second is the refill, not the burst.

variants.prompt: Refill is 10 per second and capacity is 50. The bucket is empty. How many tokens does it hold after 3 idle seconds?

mistakes.feedback: Three seconds of refill does not reach the cap.

variants.title: Run the bucket
variants.context: A token bucket stores up to b credits and refills at r per second. An operation with cost c is admitted only when c tokens are available. Over an interval T, a conforming flow cannot exceed r×T + b.
variants.prompt: Refill is 10 per second and capacity is 50. Over a 10-second interval, what is the maximum number of conforming operations of cost 1?
variants.explanation: 10 × 10 + 50 = 150 operations at most in that window.

mistakes.feedback: Multiply the refill by the full interval.

variants.title: Choose the algorithm
variants.context: Token bucket: burst plus bounded average. Leaky-bucket shaper: bounded queue released at a fixed rate. Fixed window: simple quota with a boundary burst. Sliding window: exact recent-history bound with state costs.
variants.prompt: A valid burst from a mobile app must pass immediately, while the long-term rate stays bounded. Which algorithm?
options: Leaky-bucket shaper.
Fixed window.
Token bucket.
optionFeedback: A shaper delays the burst.
A fixed window may reject a valid burst at the boundary.
Stored credit admits the burst; refill bounds the average.
variants.explanation: Prefer stored credit when controlled bursts are valid.

variants.title: Choose the algorithm
variants.context: Token bucket: burst plus bounded average. Leaky-bucket shaper: bounded queue released at a fixed rate. Fixed window: simple quota with a boundary burst. Sliding window: exact recent-history bound with state costs.
variants.prompt: Output must be smoothed and callers tolerate queueing. Which algorithm, and what must be explicit?
options: A token bucket sized for the peak burst.
A sliding log over the last sixty seconds.
A leaky-bucket shaper with bounded queue and wait.
optionFeedback: A token bucket admits bursts rather than smoothing.
A sliding log bounds history; it does not smooth departures.
Shaping releases work at a fixed rate from a bounded queue.
variants.hint: Is delay part of the contract?
variants.explanation: RFC 3290 distinguishes shaping from metering; bound the queue.

variants.title: Choose the algorithm
variants.context: Token bucket: burst plus bounded average. Leaky-bucket shaper: bounded queue released at a fixed rate. Fixed window: simple quota with a boundary burst. Sliding window: exact recent-history bound with state costs.
variants.prompt: A fixed window of 100 per minute lets a client send 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00. What is this?
options: A client bug that ignores the window.
Impossible; the limiter would block it.
The boundary burst inherent to fixed windows.
optionFeedback: The client is within each window.
The limiter allows it; each window counted only 100 requests.
Two allowances either side of a reset concentrate at the boundary.
variants.hint: What happens at the window reset?
variants.explanation: Use a fixed window only when the boundary burst is safe.

variants.title: Make one decision
variants.context: A distributed limiter must make one decision, not three racing operations: derive a trusted key, evaluate atomically, apply overflow behavior, return a usable contract.
variants.prompt: Three request handlers share a limit. Put the distributed decision in order.

items.text: Return a contract that explains scope and recovery without leaking topology.
Derive a trusted key from authenticated identity, resource, policy version, and tenant boundary.
Refill or expire prior usage and compare cost with credit as one atomic state transition.
Admit, reject, or enter a bounded queue, with the limiter timeout below the protected operation’s budget.

variants.hint: Read-decide-update must be atomic, or handlers spend the same credit.
variants.explanation: Key → atomic evaluation → overflow behavior → usable response. Redis INCR with expiry or Lua is one implementation.

variants.title: Make one decision
variants.context: A distributed limiter must make one decision, not three racing operations: derive a trusted key, evaluate atomically, apply overflow behavior, return a usable contract.
variants.prompt: A limiter is being moved from per-instance memory to a shared store. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Evaluate atomically in the shared store.
Normalize proxy signals and derive the trusted key.
Apply overflow behavior with a bounded limiter timeout.

variants.hint: Per-instance counters were never one decision.
variants.explanation: The store must not become an unbounded synchronous dependency; keep its timeout short.

variants.title: Make one decision
variants.context: A distributed limiter must make one decision, not three racing operations: derive a trusted key, evaluate atomically, apply overflow behavior, return a usable contract.
variants.prompt: The limiter store times out. Put the steps in order, including the deliberate failure choice.

items.text: Apply the chosen failure policy: fail closed or fail open under a bounded emergency policy.
Attempt the atomic evaluation; it times out under the limiter budget.
Return the contract the policy defines.

variants.hint: Failure behavior is chosen in advance, not improvised.
variants.explanation: Fail closed protects the dependency; fail open protects availability. Choose deliberately.

variants.title: Shape the policy
variants.context: Every decision needs an explicit identity, resource, cost, time model, and overflow behavior. An IP can hide many users behind NAT; expensive operations should cost weighted units; limiter-store failure must fail closed or open deliberately.
variants.prompt: A limit keyed by client IP blocks an entire office behind one NAT. What is wrong?
options: Key on a trusted user, API key, or tenant.
The limit is set too high for an office.
Nothing; IP is a fine identity here.
optionFeedback: Identity must be a trusted signal.
The key, not the number, is wrong.
One IP can be many people, and one person can rotate IPs.
variants.explanation: Name the caller with a trusted identity.

variants.title: Shape the policy
variants.context: Every decision needs an explicit identity, resource, cost, time model, and overflow behavior. An IP can hide many users behind NAT; expensive operations should cost weighted units; limiter-store failure must fail closed or open deliberately.
variants.prompt: Batch requests of 1,000 rows cost the same as single-row reads under the limit. What is missing?
options: A smaller window over the same count.
Weighted cost: charge units by rows or bytes.
A separate endpoint for batch reads.
optionFeedback: Windows do not fix cost.
Request counts hide real load.
Moving batches elsewhere still charges each one as a single request.
variants.hint: Does every request consume equal downstream work?
variants.explanation: Charge a cost that reflects the protected resource.

variants.title: Shape the policy
variants.context: Every decision needs an explicit identity, resource, cost, time model, and overflow behavior. An IP can hide many users behind NAT; expensive operations should cost weighted units; limiter-store failure must fail closed or open deliberately.
options: Nothing; the number says all of it.
Only the time unit the count applies to.
Who shares it, what it costs, and overflow behavior.
optionFeedback: Four dimensions are missing.
Time is one of several.
A limit is incomplete without identity, resource, cost, time model, and overflow.
variants.hint: What must a complete decision specify?
variants.explanation: Every decision needs identity, resource, cost, time model, and overflow behavior.

variants.title: Define overflow
variants.context: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe; use a bounded queue only when delayed work is part of the product; never create an unbounded hidden backlog.
variants.prompt: A synchronous checkout call exceeds its limit and waiting would break the user’s deadline. What should happen?
options: Reject now, with a usable recovery contract.
Queue it until capacity frees up.
Admit it anyway, since checkout matters.
optionFeedback: When waiting is unsafe, reject now.
Unbounded hidden backlogs are never acceptable.
Exempting the most valuable path is how a limit stops protecting anything.
variants.explanation: Rejection with recovery guidance is a legitimate outcome.

variants.title: Define overflow
variants.context: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe; use a bounded queue only when delayed work is part of the product; never create an unbounded hidden backlog.
variants.prompt: Report generation is part of the product contract and can run later. What overflow behavior fits?
options: A bounded queue with a maximum wait.
Immediate rejection with a retry hint.
An unbounded queue that never rejects.
optionFeedback: Delayed work that is part of the contract can queue, with bounds.
Rejection wastes valid work.
Unbounded queues hide backlogs.
variants.hint: Is delay acceptable, and is it bounded?
variants.explanation: Never create an unbounded hidden backlog.

variants.title: Define overflow
variants.context: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe; use a bounded queue only when delayed work is part of the product; never create an unbounded hidden backlog.
variants.prompt: Is rate limiting a complete denial-of-service defense?
options: Yes, if the limits are tuned tightly.
Yes, as long as it fails closed.
No. It bounds accepted work, nothing more.
optionFeedback: Tight limits still admit work from a large enough set of distinct callers.
Failure mode does not make it complete.
It is a control on accepted work.
variants.explanation: Rate limiting is admission policy, not proof of capacity.
